newsitem.title: USA: House panel works on U.S. health legislation.
newsitem.headline: House panel works on U.S. health legislation.

text.p: A House subcommittee worked on Medicare and Medicaid overhauls Tuesday, seeking savings in the two big health programmes while introducing a new plan to cover about half of America's uninsured children.

The Medicaid plan, one of the most significant domestic initiatives to move through Congress this year, included $15 billion in overall savings over five years but also added $16 billion to let states expand health coverage for up to half of the estimated 10 million uninsured children.

Earlier, it worked on a plan to save $115 billion from the Medicare programme for children older than 5, mostly by slowing payments to doctors and other health care providers and offering more managed care options to patients.
Both health programmes are big pieces of the agreement between the Republican-controlled Congress and the White House to balance the federal budget in five years.

The House Ways and Means Committee Monday approved a similar Medicare bill. The Senate Finance Committee was working on its own version, and a draft of a staff plan included a provision to gradually raise the age of Medicare eligibility to 67 from 65.

"It's not a surprise. This idea has been floating around with no hearings, no research and no answer to what people are supposed to do who then can't get access," said John Rother of the American Association of Retired Persons.

In the Commerce subcommittee, Republicans defeated several attempts by Democrats to kill a pilot project of Medical Savings Accounts (MSAs) that would allow people to set aside money in tax-free accounts to meet future health needs.

Republicans said the accounts, used with high-deductible insurance policies that kick in for medical catastrophies, would make Medicare patients smart health care shoppers. Democrats said the accounts will draw away the healthiest and wealthiest seniors and undermine Medicare by leaving it with only the poorest and sickest patients.

In a vote that crossed party lines, the subcommittee backed an amendment by Representative Tom Coburn, an Oklahoma Republican and physician, that would make sure doctors decide how long patients remain in the hospital, instead of leaving such decisions to managed care plan administrators or clerks.
Lawmakers earlier backed setting minimum requirements for the length of stay in a hospital after giving birth or having a mastectomy.

The Republican Medicaid plan would provide $2.6 billion a year in grants that states could use to expand care to poor children. The programme would be voluntary and states would have to contribute funds of their own. But they would have latitude in designing their programmes, which could include vouchers, managed care, direct aid or other methods.
Governors could expand existing Medicaid programmes to reach more children, including those in families with incomes up to 150 percent of poverty, about $25,000 for a family of four.
Children's advocates said the plan was too broad, allowing states to use the new money to replace funds lost under Medicaid.
In another significant change from the House, the Senate Finance Medicare bill would require seniors to pay $5 for each visit by a home health provider though the overall payment would be capped.
